narrative:
The model determined that you have an 88.3% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and this probability is quite high, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Being in the bottom decile, far below the average ranking of accepted students, signaled that you struggled to keep pace with your peers later in your studies. Your first-year ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure; again, a bottom-decile placement contrasted sharply with the much stronger average performance of admitted students. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most influential feature, but it worked mildly in the opposite direction. At 2.90 it is below the 3.23 average of accepted students, yet the model still saw this as one of the few elements that slightly increased the chance you might pass.

Taken together, the consistently low class rankings outweighed the modest positive signal from your GPA and led to the high predicted risk of bar exam failure.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic performance and bar-exam readiness. Consider retaking key courses, seeking targeted tutoring, or enrolling in a structured bar-preparation program before reapplying. Improving your class rank and test scores will directly address the factors that worked against you. (218 words)
